Unit 5 - Causal Diagrams

James Flynn

September 16, 2026

Recap

  • So far we’ve worked on coding basics and data viz
  • This week we are thinking about how to use these tools for causal inference
  • We want to find ways to isolate just the variation that represents the effect of X on Y

Causal inference requires modeling

  • We will now think more about how we can identify causality in data
  • Part of that will necessarily require us to have a model
    • Doesn’t need to be a big structural model
    • Doesn’t necessarily even need to be written down

Models

  • We have to have a model to get at causality
  • A model is our way of understanding the world. It’s our idea of what we think the data-generating process is
  • Models can be informal or formal
    • Structural papers typically have rigorous formal models
    • Reduced-form papers often have a conceptual framework section instead
  • Even if your paper does not have a model, you need to have one in mind before you start running regressions
  • All models are oversimplifications. Tradeoff between tractability and usefulness

Models

  • Once we do have a model, though, that model will tell us exactly how we can find a causal effect
  • (if it’s possible; sometimes the model says that to identify we must do something impossible)
  • If we have a source of identified variation in how X was assigned, we may be able to use that variation to get a good estimate of the treatment effect

Example

  • Let’s work through a basic example where we know the data generating process
# Is your company in tech? Let's say 30% of firms are
df <- tibble(tech = sample(c(0,1),500,replace=T,prob=c(.7,.3))) %>%
  #Tech firms on average spend $3mil more defending IP lawsuits
  mutate(IP.spend = 3*tech+runif(500,min=0,max=4)) %>%
  #Tech firms also have higher profits. But IP lawsuits lower profits
  mutate(log.profit = 2*tech - .3*IP.spend + rnorm(500,mean=2))
# Now let's check for how profit and IP.spend are correlated!
cor(df$log.profit,df$IP.spend)
## [1] 0.1472215
  • Uh-oh! Truth is negative relationship, but data says positive!!

Example

  • We want to know the causal effect of IP lawsuits on profits
  • Now we can ask: what do we know about this situation?
  • How do we suspect the data was generated? (ignoring for a moment that we know already)
    • We know that being a tech company leads you to have to spend more money on IP lawsuits
    • We know that tech companies generally have high profits
    • We know that IP lawsuits lower your profits

Example

  • Part of what we get when we calculate cor(df$log.profit,df$IP.spend) is the influence of being a tech company
  • If we remove the influence being a tech company has on both IP spending and profits, what’s left over should be the actual, negative, effect of IP lawsuits
  • What if we had a more formal model that could tell us what to do in lots of situations

Causal Diagrams

  • Enter the causal diagram!
  • A causal diagram is a way of writing down your model that lets you figure out what you need to do to find your causal effect of interest
    • Also know as Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs
  • All you need to do to make a causal diagram is write down all the important features of the data generating process, and also write down what you think causes what.

Example

  • We know that being a tech company leads you to have to spend more money on IP lawsuits
  • We know that being a tech company leads you to have higher profits
  • We know that IP lawsuits lower your profits

Identification

  • We have encoded everything we know about this particular little world in our diagram
  • Not only can we see our assumptions, but we can see how they fit together
  • And if we want to isolate the effect of IP.spend on profit, we can figure that out too
  • We’re identifying just one of those arrows, the one IP.spend -> profit, and seeing what the effect is on that arrow!
  • If we can shut down the other arrows, there’s only one path you can walk on the diagram to get from treatment to outcome - only one kind of variation left, and it MUST be the causal effect you want

Controlling

  • Imagine we’re looking at that relationship within color
  • Here, being a tech company is a confounder

Causal Diagrams

  • The diagram that told us to control for tech, but we could have gotten there on our own
  • It’s going to turn out that diagrams can tell us how to identify things in much more complex circumstances

What is a mediator?

  • Here is a DGP
set.seed(12)
x <- rnorm(10000)
m <- rnorm(10000) + x
y <- rnorm(10000) + 2*x + 3*m
  • What is the direct effect of x on y?
  • What will we get if we regress x on y?

Regress x on y

lm1 <- lm(y~x)
summary(lm1)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = y ~ x)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -10.8240  -2.1565  -0.0283   2.1507  10.9876 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  0.02126    0.03173    0.67    0.503    
## x            4.97192    0.03168  156.95   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 3.173 on 9998 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.7113, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7113 
## F-statistic: 2.463e+04 on 1 and 9998 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

What happens when we control for a mediator?

lm1 <- lm(y~x+m)
summary(lm1)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = y ~ x + m)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -4.4072 -0.6776 -0.0064  0.6742  4.6133 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 0.001679   0.009936   0.169    0.866    
## x           1.975400   0.014000 141.101   <2e-16 ***
## m           3.016492   0.009946 303.295   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
##

Mediator DAG

Mediator examples

  • Education → Health Knowledge → Health Outcomes
  • Minimum Wage → Hours Worked → Total Earnings
  • Exercise Program → Weight Loss → Blood Pressure
  • Smoking Ban → Secondhand Smoke Exposure → Infant Health

What is a collider?

set.seed(12)
looks <- rnorm(10000)
talent <- rnorm(10000)
movie_star <- looks + talent > 2
df <- tibble(looks = looks, talent = talent, movie_star = movie_star)

Scatter plot

What happens in the regression

# Unconditional regression: talent on looks, full sample
summary(lm(talent ~ looks, data = df))$coefficients["looks",]
##     Estimate   Std. Error      t value     Pr(>|t|) 
## -0.006619555  0.009973988 -0.663681909  0.506909223
# Controlling for a collider in the regression
summary(lm(talent ~ looks + movie_star, data = df))$coefficients["looks",]
##      Estimate    Std. Error       t value      Pr(>|t|) 
## -1.777902e-01  9.776199e-03 -1.818603e+01  9.838367e-73

Collider DAG

Causal Diagrams

  • Can’t we just look at the data to see what we need to control for?
  • After all, that would free us from having to make all those assumptions and figure out our model
  • No!!!
  • Why? Because for a given set of data that we see, there are many different data generating processes that could have made it
  • Each requiring different kinds of adjustments in order to get it right

Causal Diagrams

  • We observe that profit (y), IP.spend (x), and tech (z) are all related… which is it?

Causal Diagrams

  • With only the data to work with we have no way of knowing which of those is true
  • Maybe IP.spend causes companies to be tech companies (in 2, 3, 6)
  • We know that’s silly because we have an idea of what the model is
  • If you started by noticing that \(corr(tech,IP.spend)>0\), you could make this mistake

  3. Do any of the assumptions seem wrong?
